did_you_know.text: The name of the book, 'Bamidbar' (In the Wilderness), comes directly from the opening verse, indicating the geographical setting for most of the events described within it.
The census described in this chapter took place on the first day of the second month in the second year after the Exodus, exactly one month after the Tabernacle was completed and consecrated.
The phrase 'take the head' (meaning 'take a census') is not just about counting, but also signifies the importance and honor of each individual counted among the people.
Only men aged twenty and older, defined as 'all those who go out to war,' were counted in the census, indicating a distinct military aspect to this count.
Each tribe had an appointed leader, who played an important role in assisting Moses and Aaron with conducting the census and organizing the people.
Names like 'Zurishaddai' (leader of the tribe of Simeon) contain one of God's names, 'Shaddai,' meaning 'my rock is Shaddai,' indicating faith and trust in God.
Nahshon ben Amminadab, the leader of the tribe of Judah, is remembered in tradition as the first to jump into the Red Sea before it parted.
The phrase 'they registered themselves by their families' suggests a meticulous process of recording and proving family lineage, not just a simple headcount.
The tribe of Judah had the largest number of men fit for military service (74,600), suggesting its leading and strong position among the tribes.
The tribe of Manasseh was the smallest tribe counted (32,200) when compared to the other tribes enumerated for military service.
The total number of men fit for military service was 603,550, a vast number that required complex logistical planning for their journeys and encampment.
The Levites were not counted with the other tribes, because their role was not to go to war but to perform sacred service in the Tabernacle.
God's command not to count the tribe of Levi among the other Israelites emphasizes their unique and distinct destiny apart from the rest of the people.
The Levites were entrusted with all the work of the Tabernacle, including carrying its vessels, dismantling it, and setting it up, which was a demanding physical and operational role.
The warning 'and the unauthorized person who comes near shall be put to death' highlights the sanctity of the Tabernacle and the danger involved in approaching it without explicit authorization.
The Israelites camped 'each man by his own camp and each man by his own standard,' indicating a detailed and well-organized camp structure, with specific banners for each tribe.
The Levites camped around the Tabernacle of the Testimony, serving as a human barrier that protected it and safeguarded the Israelites from the sin of unauthorized approach.
The concluding verse of the chapter emphasizes the complete obedience of the Israelites to God's instructions: 'According to all that the Lord commanded Moses, so they did.'
